title: Space to Ground: Scientific Ride: 11/04/2022
description: NASA's Space to Ground is your weekly update on what's happening aboard the International Space Station.

transcript.text: Welcome to Space to Ground, I’m Jaden Jennings.
Northrop Grumman has named the next Cygnus mission to the International Space Station
in honor of Dr. Sally Ride, astronaut, physicist, advocate for diversity in science,
and the first American woman to fly into space.
The NG-18 mission is scheduled to launch on Sunday November 6,
from the Wallops Flight Facility in Virginia.
The spacecraft will deliver more than 8,200 pounds of cargo
for the station's Expedition 68 crew as well as several key science experiments.
Onboard Cygnus, the OVOSPACE Investigation will study possible changes
in ovarian cell development in microgravity.
The study will use bovine cell cultures in order to understand those changes.
As we work toward a permanent human presence on the Moon,
this research seeks to identify possible treatments
to protect reproductive health off the planet,
and could also improve or restore fertility in people here on Earth.
Another study that will fly on Cygnus will look
for solutions to prevent a disastrous event after wildfires.
The effects of wildfires are devastating, causing loss of property, and loss of lives.
Even more damage can happen months after the event.
When a wildfire burns plants, combusted chemicals create
a thin layer of soil that repels rainwater.
Rain then erodes the soil, which can lead to catastrophic mudflows
that carry heavy boulders and debris downhill, causing significant damage.
The Post-Wildfire Mudflow Micro-Structure investigation
will evaluate the composition of these mudflows.
Microgravity could unlock new understanding of these phenomena,
which may improve modeling and prediction of their behavior.
What we learn could support the development of ways
to prevent and reduce catastrophic post-fire events.
And now, it’s time for Nachos…but not the type that you eat.
The Nanosat Atmospheric Chemistry Hyperspectral Observation System,
or NACHOS for short, flew to the Space Station in February.
Weighing just 13 pounds, this protype instrument could eventually
make it easier to monitor volcanic activity and air quality in cities,
neighborhoods and power plants.
NACHOS will be the topic on this week’s edition of “Houston, We Have a Podcast”
You can find it on Apple podcasts, Google podcasts, or Soundcloud,
or find it on the NASA Johnson Space Center social media channels on Facebook, Instagram,
and Twitter.
And that’s Space to Ground for now.
Thank you so much for watching,
and we’ll see you next week.
